title: TB8-26864
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): He appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) is a citizen of Pakistan. He appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.

The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

The Appellant alleged before the RPD that after working in Greece from 2011 to 2013, he returned to Pakistan and started a small business. In August 2013 he was approached at his business by four men collecting donations for the group Lashkar-e-Taiba. These men demanded ?XXXX XXXX XXXX, which the Appellant paid after one week on the advice of his friend. His friend also advised him not to go to the police because the police always protect these groups.

The Appellant was aware that other store owners in his town were victims of extortion and he tried to convince them slowly and gradually about standing up to the extortionists. In XXXX 2014 two men came to his store and told him that they knew what he was doing and beat him. They demanded a further donation of ?XXXX XXXX XXXX and gave him a deadline of three days to pay. The Appellant did not know what to do. After a couple of days he was chased by some people but was able to escape and went to a friend's home before returning home. At home he was advised that the men had been there and fired at their walls and kicked the door. The men told his mother that they would kill the Appellant.

The Appellant moved to his aunt's house in another town, but was chased by two men on the street. He was able to hide in a bakery, but was worried about this new situation. The Appellant moved to Sialkot and began to make arrangements to leave Pakistan. He left in XXXX 2014 and eventually arrived in the US on XXXX XXXX, 2015. He made a claim for asylum in the US, but was unable to get a work permit. He eventually decided to leave the US and come to Canada in XXXX 2018.

The Appellant's claim for refugee protection was heard on August 10, 2018. In a decision dated October 4, 2018 the RPD rejected his claim finding that the Appellant had not established that state protection was unavailable and that there were credibility concerns regarding omissions from his Basis of Claim (BOC).
The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in its assessment of state protection. ANALYSIS State Protection

The RPD found that the evidence in the record did not show that the Appellant was unable to receive operationally adequate state protection in Pakistan. The RPD noted that the Appellant never made any attempt to obtain protection after six incidents. The RPD found that the Appellant did not provide clear and convincing proof of Pakistan's inability to protect him. The RPD rejected the Appellant's explanation that going to the police was never an option because the government colluded with the Lashkar-e-Taiba and other store owners who had gone to the police seeking protection had been murdered, as these murderers were not mentioned in his BOC narrative. The RPD rejected the Appellant's explanation for this omission, which was that the BOC was only about his own experiences.

The RPD found that despite the Appellant's testimony that terrorist perpetrators are always listed as unknown persons in police reports, the police report he did submit into evidence regarding a storeowner who had been murdered shows that it was the brother of the storeowner who reported the attacker as an unknown person and that the police registered the case and initiated an investigation.

The RPD found that the Appellant's explanation about the omission of the murder of a storeowner in his town from his BOC was contradictory and not credible. The RPD noted that he stated that he heard about this incident in XXXX 2017, which was before his BOC was signed on February 10, 2018. The Appellant's first explanation was that his BOC had already been submitted when he heard about this incident. When it was pointed out to him that the incident preceded the submission of his BOC he then stated that he actually heard about the story in XXXX 2018. The RPD noted that the DVD provided by the Appellant about the storeowner's murder showed no link between the Appellant and the victim and gave it a little probative value.

The RPD considered the affidavits from family and friends to support the allegations and noted that the mother's affidavit stated that the Lashkar-e-Taiba was looking for him at the family home as late as XXXX 2018. The RPD considered the Appellant's assertion that the Lashkar-e-Taiba had a vast operational network in collusion with the Pakistani government and was able to track him down at his aunt's home in XXXX, a four hour drive from his home in XXXX, when he went there in XXXX 2014. The RPD found that if the Lashkar-e-Taiba did have a vast network as alleged, it was not plausible that the group would not know that he had left the country in XXXX 2014 and would continue going to his family home several times over the years looking for him. The RPD concluded that the Lashkar-e-Taiba had no continuing interest in the Appellant.

The Appellant argues that the RPD ignored the efficacy of police in providing protection in Pakistan. He submits that the documentary evidence states that the efficacy of the police varies greatly by district ranging from reasonably good to effective and that Pakistan's police system suffers severe deficiencies in many areas including equipment, technology, personnel training and intelligence capability. He submits that Pakistan's police force is under resourced, poorly trained and has a poor human rights record.

The Appellant argues that he did not go to the police for protection because the police would have ganged up with the Lashkar-e-Taiba to secure some of the extortion money and would not provide protection.

The RAD has reviewed the record and has conducted an independent assessment of the evidence. The RAD notes that the country condition documentary evidence indicates that the Lashkar-e-Talba is an anti-Indian group focused on the Kashmir dispute and that it operates with the alleged support of the Pakistani military and the intelligence agency Inter-Services Intelligence.1 It is noted in a BBC article that people who oppose pro-Pakistan groups such as Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammad are "threatened, beaten up and arrested". According to Freedom House, the tension between pro-Pakistan groups and pro-independence groups has led to increased attacks against Shiites.2

The RAD has considered the documentary evidence regarding terrorist financing. It is noted in the Canadian document Terrorist Financing Assessment 2018 3 that the Lashkar-e-Taiba relies on diverse revenue streams and a significant portion of the group's financial and material support originates from the state of Pakistan, as well as charitable donations from the Gulf States, charities and expatriate communities and businessmen. It is also noted that the group systematically exploits its non-militant arm, Jamaat-ud-dawa, for its social welfare networks. The group also diverts revenues and tuition fees raised from its Islamic institutions, medical clinics and services. It is noted that other profitable illicit activities include counterfeiting currency and drug trafficking. Lashkar-e-Taiba also relies heavily on informal international money transfers and cash couriers. The RAD notes that not included in its fundraising activities is extortion of local businesses. The RAD notes that the Terrorist Financing Assessment 2018 document contains information about other organizations, such as the Haqqani Network, extorting and levying taxes on local, regional and international businesses and citizens in its area of control. However this does not appear to be a fundraising method used by the Lashkar-e-Taiba.

The RAD finds that there is no country condition documentary evidence on the record showing that extortion of local businessmen is a fundraising method of the Lashkar-e-Taiba. Furthermore, the police report and news item relating to the murder of a local businessman4 does not indicate who the perpetrator was or the name of the organization the perpetrator belonged to. Although the Appellant alleged that other businessmen in his area had been targeted and killed by the Lashkar-e-Taiba, he has provided no supporting documentation regarding these murderers.

The RAD notes that the Appellant has provided several affidavits which reflect the information contained in his BOC, that he was extorted by members of the Lashkar-e-Taiba. The RAD will accept on a balance of probabilities that members of this organizations did attempt to extort money from the Appellant based on these affidavits. However, the RAD finds that this is a localized situation as it is not part of the documented methods used by the Lashkar-e-Taiba to raise funds.

The RAD finds that the affidavit of the brother of the businessman who was killed5 has limited value as the information contained in this affidavit is not supported by the police report and news item noted earlier. Furthermore, the RAD notes that it is stated in the affidavit that the Appellant was a good friend of his brother who was killed in XXXX 2017. The RAD finds it suspect that the Appellant would not mention the death of a similarly-situated person who was a good friend in his BOC. The RAD notes that question 2 (a) asks whether persons in similar situations experienced such harm, mistreatment or threats and to indicate the dates, names and places, wherever possible. Given this direction, and the Appellant's close relationship with the murdered man, the RAD agrees with the RPD that the Appellant's explanation that he thought he just had to write about himself, was not reasonable. Furthermore, the Appellant was represented by counsel in the preparation of his BOC. The RAD finds that little weight can be assigned to the brother's affidavit given this omission from the BOC and the lack of information contained in the supporting documents regarding who were the perpetrators of the crime.

The RAD has considered whether the Appellant could have availed himself of state protection in his hometown of XXXX. The Appellant has argued that he could not go to the police at any time because the state was connected to the Lashkar-e-Taiba and because Pakistan's police force is under-resourced, poorly trained and has a poor human rights record. The RAD notes that the documentary evidence does indicate that the Lashkar-e-Taiba operates with the alleged support of the Pakistani military and the intelligence agency Inter-Services Intelligence. The RAD finds, given this information, that it was reasonable that the Appellant would not approach the local police in his particular circumstances.

The RAD finds that the Appellant has not established on a balance of probabilities that the individuals seeking him out have the ability or will to find him anywhere in Pakistan. The RAD notes that the Appellant testified that the agents of persecution discovered him when he was living with his aunt in XXXX for XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX from XXXX XXXX, 2014 to XXXX 2014. He then moved to Sialkot to make travel arrangements to leave Pakistan in August 2014 and remained there until November 2014 when he left Pakistan. There is no evidence that he was discovered while living in that city for approximately three to four months. Furthermore, the affidavit from the Appellant's father states that people are still looking for him and several times "slammed on our doors" in search of him. It is stated that the last time members of Lashkar-e-Taiba looked for the Appellant was in XXXX 2018. After considering this information, the RAD finds that the Appellant has not demonstrated that the individuals who seek him out have the power to find him anywhere as they did not locate him in Sialkot, which is a much larger municipality than XXXX, and, as late as 2018, were not aware that he had exited the country in 2014. Despite the information that the Lashkar-e-Taiba operates with the alleged support of the Pakistani military and the intelligence agency Inter-Services Intelligence, it does not appear that the individuals seeking him out availed themselves of that support if it did indeed exist. The RAD therefore finds that the Appellant has a viable internal flight alternative (IFA) elsewhere in the country. Internal Flight Alternative

The RPD found that the Appellant had not established that the core elements of the claim were credible or plausible and did not therefore consider the issue of internal flight alternative. However the RPD did note in its decision that the Appellant had stated that he would be tracked anywhere in Pakistan including Karachi, which is over XXXX XXXX XXXX km away from his home.
The RAD requested submissions from the Appellant in regard to the issue of a proposed IFA in Karachi or Lahore, which were received by the RAD on March 25, 2019.

The Appellant argues that he does not have a viable IFA anywhere in Pakistan, including Karachi or Lahore because of his fear of the militant group in Pakistan and his belief that this group could target him anywhere in the country. The Appellant submits that the documentary evidence regarding the Lashkar-e-Taiba states that the organization is based near Lahore and that there are several thousand members. He submits that Lahore cannot be a viable IFA due to geographical reasons, and that Karachi is not a viable IFA given the size of the group.

The Appellant argues that Lashkar e Taiba has significant ties to global militant Islamist organizations and that it has assisted Al-Qaeda. He submits that Lashkar-e-Taiba has formed alliances with Harkatul-Mujhaideen (HM), Hizb-ul-Mujhaideen (HuM), Jaish-e-Muhammed (JeM) and Harkatul-Jihadi-lslami (Hull) against Indian military assets in India-controlled Kashmir. The Appellant argues that given the ties with other militant groups, there is a high likelihood that he would be persecuted by the Lashkar-e-Taiba or its allies. Ordinary Pakistanis, students and those perceived to be opposing the Taliban and other groups, or are not following sharia law, have been subjected to violence by these groups. He argues that the documentary evidence states that the authorities do not adequately protect vulnerable individuals, and have refrained from promptly investigating perpetrators of activities including abduction for ransom by groups like the Haqqani Network and Lashkar-e-Taiba.

The RAD has reviewed the record and finds that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Karachi. The RAD notes that the country condition documentary evidence states that simply living in an area occupied, either wholly or partly, by the Pakistani Taliban or other militant groups does not give rise to a protection need. In general the risks from the Pakistani Taliban or other militant groups will depend on the particular profile of the person, the nature of the threat and how far it would extend. Primary targets include political and/or tribal leaders, security forces and minority religious groups. However, ordinary Pakistanis, including students and those perceived to be opposing the Taliban and other militant groups or not following sharia law, have also been subjected to violence by these groups. The risk will be highest in areas where those armed anti-government groups are operating or have control. Those main areas are: Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (formerly known as North West Frontier Province); the semi-autonomous Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA) that have a strong Taliban presence; and Baluchistan, where separatists are seeking greater political autonomy and control over local mineral resources.6

The RAD has considered the Appellant's particular situation. As noted earlier, the RAD has found that the threat to the Appellant was localized to members of the Lashkar-e-Taiba in his home area of XXXX. Although these people allegedly discovered the Appellant in 2014 near his aunt's home approximately four hours distance away by car, there is no information in the record that they were able to discover his whereabouts at any other time, or that he had left Pakistan in 2014. Furthermore, despite having discovered in August 2014 that he was in XXXX, there is no evidence on the record that they knew where his aunt lived or that they visited her home at any time looking for him. The RAD notes that the Appellant's family has continued to live in XXXX and other than people coming to the family home asking about him, there is no evidence in the record that any attempts were made to harm family members in order to locate the Appellant. The RAD has also considered that the Appellant was not a high profile opponent of the Lashkar-e-Taiba; rather he was a small business owner who did not want to pay extortion money. The RAD finds that there is insufficient information in the record to establish that members of this group would aggressively seek him out all over the country using its ties with the Pakistan government in order to locate him so that he could pay a bribe of ?XXXX, especially since the Appellant has been out of the country for five years and has had no contact with members of this group since he left Pakistan.

The RAD has further considered the documentary evidence showing that the fundraising activities of the Lashkar-e-Taiba do not include extortion of business owners and are focused on raising funds through legitimate means through schools, international remittances and donations and through less legitimate means such as drug trafficking and counterfeiting currency.7

The RAD finds that Karachi, which is a huge city with a population of approximately 25 million people, is a viable IFA for the Appellant. It is noted in the documentary evidence that security operations in Karachi have significantly reduced the level of militant and sectarian violence in recent years and that there are areas of the city that are relatively safe. The documentary evidence indicates that large urban centres such as Karachi, Islamabad and Lahore tend to have ethnically and religiously diverse populations, and offer a level of anonymity for people seeking refuge from violence by non-state actors. 8

The RAD notes that the Appellant has alleged that Lashkar-e-Taiba is connected with the Pakistani government and police forces, and the country condition documentation indicate that it operates with the alleged support of the Pakistani military and the intelligence agency Inter-Services Intelligence. However, as noted earlier, the evidence in the record does not indicate that the local members of the Lashkar-e-Taiba in Gujranwala who were extorting money from the Appellant availed themselves of the resources of the Pakistani military and intelligence service given that they did not locate the Appellant in Sialkot where he resided for over three months and were not aware that he had left the country. The only evidence of continuing interest in the Appellant by the agents of persecution was that they went to his family home in XXXX and asked about him. Given this history, the RAD finds on a balance of probabilities that the Lashkar-e-Taiba would not seek out the Appellant in Karachi should he relocate to that city. The RAD furthermore notes the documentary evidence which states that a lack of resources limited the government's ability to implement effective control and enforce the law.9 The RAD does not find it plausible in these circumstances that the government would use its limited resources to search all over Pakistan for a person who does not have a high profile, in order to satisfy low-level members of a banned terrorist organization who wish to extort money from a business owner.

The RAD finds that the Appellant could live in Karachi without fear that the agents of persecution would find him in that city. The RAD further finds it would be reasonable for the Appellant to live in Karachi. He is a XXXX with both XXXX and XXXX XXXX. He is well educated and speaks Urdu, English and Punjabi. As noted earlier, Karachi is a very large city and has ethnically and religiously diverse communities. The RAD finds it reasonable to expect that the Appellant would either be able to find work or set up his own business in Karachi, that he and his family would be able to find a residence, and his children would be able to attend school.

The RAD finds, after considering all of the evidence, and given the Appellant's past and present circumstances, that Karachi is a viable IFA and that there is not a serious possibility that he would suffer persecution in Karachi or on a balance of probabilities a personal risk of harm in Karachi.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
